audit.reason: Vattel renders Wolff's Prolegomena §4 closely: necessary law of nations contains what natural law prescribes to nations, binding them as it binds men.
Vattel renders Wolff's definition of the perfection of a nation and of its perfect state almost clause for clause.
Vattel reproduces Wolff's two steps: perfection as the accord of a thing's parts toward one end, and the nation as a multitude united in civil society.
Wolff's ruler, holding the nation's rights, represents his nation in its dealings, which Vattel states as the sovereign's representative character.
Vattel translates Wolff's definition of jura merae facultatis almost word for word (use or not use as one pleases, free of all constraint).
That the ruler should protect the sciences and arts is a general maxim; Wolff's definitional sentence gives nothing specific to Vattel's passage.
Vattel follows Wolff's § 135 in deriving love of country from the citizen's undertaking to promote the common good, after the self-love step.
Vattel's clause renders Wolff's proposition that a nation must love itself nearly word for word, so it is closer than a loose paraphrase.
Same Wolffian argument that private war is not tolerated because judges render each his right, applied to the duel.

Wolff's section is about the ruler's freedom to admit a foreigner as citizen or resident, not a definition of inhabitants; it overlaps with Vattel's only in the idea of allowing a foreigner to reside.
Vattel's definition of domicile renders Wolff's Latin definition word for word.
Vattel's sentence is a word-for-word rendering of Wolff's Latin, so 'translation' fits better than 'close paraphrase'.
That an owner may alienate or pledge what is its own is a stock consequence of dominion, and Wolff §484 on what nations may pledge has none of Vattel's specific argument.
Vattel's limit of sea dominion to what a nation needs for security and can make respected restates Wolff § 128 (occupation as far as dominion can be defended, the sea as a rampart).
Vattel's general principle renders Wolff's: a nation owes another what it owes itself, insofar as the other needs it and it can give it without neglecting its duties to itself.

Vattel restates Wolff's two conditions for offices of humanity (the other's need, and no neglect of duty to oneself) and goes on, as Wolff § 157 does, to the asked nation's right to judge and the grain example.
Vattel's sentence renders Wolff's thesis of par. 263 closely: no nation may refuse the offices of humanity to another because of a different religion.
Vattel's limit on offices to other nations ('sans manquer à ses devoirs envers elle-même') reproduces Wolff's 'citra neglectum officii erga se ipsam'.
Same Wolffian prohibition on hindering another nation from attaining the end of civil society, with near-identical structure.
Vattel's definition of consuls follows Wolff's clause by clause: ports, commission, guarding the nation's rights and privileges, settling merchants' disputes.
Wolff's statement that the form of the republic makes no difference to what belongs to the nation is his argument on precedence (it stands in § 243, not § 153), which Vattel restates.
The maxim that self-government is the mark of independence is general. Vattel II.57's own point, the right to repel interference, is not in Wolff § 256.
Same argument that ceding uncultivated land to incoming settlers is both a benefit to them and a gain in population and power for the nation.
Vattel restates Wolff 322: a later occupant of a vacant country cannot take the places or rights already occupied by another nation.
Same specific example: the widow's statutory portion cannot be reduced when a citizen makes his will abroad.
Vattel's definition of the droit d'aubaine translates Wolff's definition of jus albinagii clause by clause.
Vattel restates Wolff § 338's thesis that a nation keeps some right over another's property when deprived of a necessary use, clause by clause.
Vattel's definition of pactions as agreements with transitory, non-repeated performances renders Wolff's definition.
Vattel's 'répugne en soi à tout traité de protection' renders Wolff's 'foederi omni protectionis per se inest', and the bar on aiding the protector's enemies follows from it.
Vattel's sentence renders Wolff's 'nothing wins nations and their rulers more praise than entire good faith' in the same comparative structure.
Vattel's treaties fixing 'ce qui ne peut être déterminé en général par le droit naturel' render Wolff § 392's 'quae jure naturali in genere determinata non sunt' in a treaty context.
Same rule that a treaty made for the contractor and his successors is real, not personal; the wording and structure differ.
Vattel's definition of inferior powers, with magistrates and generals as examples, translates Wolff's closely.
Same specific explanation: hostages were once killed through the error that a man has a right over his own life or that the sovereign may dispose of it.
Wolff § 501: only the hostage's liberty is pledged, not his life, and the old contrary opinion assumed a right over one's own life; Vattel gives the same thesis and correction.
Wolff 504-505 lets a hostage be retained as a debtor for debts contracted while held, without breaching the release; Vattel states the same rule and adds crimes.
Both hold the hostage liable for his own acts, but Wolff's section 533 concerns his personal suretyship for the main obligation, not crimes and private debts during hostageship (Wolff section 505).
Vattel's maxim that neither party may interpret the treaty at will is Wolff's rule for treaties, with the same two-sided reasoning.
Vattel's maxim translates Wolff's 'quod sufficienter significatur, id contra ipsum pro vero habetur' word for word, though Wolff applies it to war here.
Vattel reproduces Wolff's rule that, since parties cannot be presumed to have meant to do nothing, an interpretation voiding the act is not admitted.
Same specific argument: an oath cannot give a later ally priority over an earlier ally whose treaty is unsworn.
Same sequence of duties: give each his right, repair the injury, give satisfaction for the irreparable one, give security where faith is suspect.

Both state Wolff's general voluntary-law principle that natural liberty leaves each nation to its own judgment, but Inst. 1215 applies it to the justice of both sides in war, not to trying peaceful means first.
Vattel's definition of retorsion of right renders Wolff's definition closely.
Vattel's 'participe à l'action de son sujet & s'en charge' renders Wolff's ruler who 'concurrit ad factum civis', turning the subject's act into the nation's act.
Same argument in the same order: milder means must be preferred while they suffice, reprisals are milder than war, and they must be used while they can obtain redress.
Vattel follows Wolff's sequence: enrolling another's subjects is plagium, soldiers swear an oath, deserters are severely punished, and those who promote desertion share the plagium.
Vattel's two kinds of reasons follow Wolff's definitions (justificatory reasons from right, suasive ones from utility, each 'by which it is shown').

Wolff § 631: in a doubtful cause war is lawful only to force a party that refuses accommodation into a transaction; Vattel gives the same rule, then Wolff's § 632 point that war does not decide right.
Vattel uses Wolff's specific analogy of two disputants over the truth of a proposition to show war cannot be just on both sides.
Same rule: if a power shows designs of domination and does even the slightest injury, the other nations may join to weaken it by arms.
Both concern a balance in which joined weaker powers offset the preponderant one, but Wolff's definition has none of Vattel's scale image or coalition practice.

Wolff § 711 says fair peace terms follow from the cause of war and the costs the declaring party was forced to incur; Vattel lists the same two parts: the principal subject plus reimbursement of preparation costs.
Vattel gives Wolff's two rules: whoever is granted passage repairs the damage, and the ruler sees that the injured subjects are compensated.
Same sequence as Wolff 875-876: non-resisting enemies are not to be harmed, so commanders must not permit soldiers to rape women and girls.
Vattel rejects the view that 'the manner is indifferent' and condemns poison as contrary to natural law, against Wolff's claim (§§877-878) that killing the enemy by poison is naturally licit.
Vattel takes up the case for poisoned weapons and declares them forbidden by natural law, against Wolff's claim that they are not naturally illicit.
Wolff's proposition that a nation may be punished by taking corporeal things and rights is what Vattel restates (things, rights, towns, provinces taken as punishment).
Wolff's argument that the war is not the auxiliaries' so booty is not theirs, with the same 'no difficulty' remark and the next point that the sovereign disposes of booty.
Vattel grounds postliminy, as Wolff § 894 does, in the sovereign's duty to defend subjects, with restitution of persons to all their rights and goods to their owners.
Vattel renders Wolff's paired definition of postliminy for persons and things falling back into their nation's power.

Vattel follows Wolff's note in sequence: what holds of soldiers holds of subordinate officers, who are like private persons, military law forbids acting without orders, and war's outcomes are uncertain.
Vattel's 'since the truce cannot bind subjects unless known, it must be published' restates Wolff's inference that subjects are bound only after publication (also in Grotius III.21.5).
Same argument as Wolff: a sovereign who will not punish or make restitution for private breaches takes part in them and himself violates the faith of the truce.
Wolff's specific rule that during a truce the besieged may not repair the rampart breached by enemy guns is restated by Vattel, with an echo of the enemy artillery.
Vattel gives Wolff's specific reason why a father's safe-conduct excludes wife and children (they do not usually travel with him) but recasts it with a contrast to permission to settle.
Same specific argument: a safe-conduct granted at pleasure lapses on the grantor's death because he ceases to will.
Near-translation of Wolff's rule that a ransom agreement cannot be rescinded because the captive proves richer than believed.
Vattel's claim that foreign nations may not judge between prince and subjects, grounded on non-interference, renders Wolff 1011.
The rule that the public compensates individuals whose goods are disposed of by eminent domain is common stock (Grotius, Pufendorf); Wolff states it generally, not for peace treaties.
Near-translation of Wolff's rule that matters on which the peace treaty is silent remain as they are.
Same specific rule as Wolff: a peace treaty may include stipulations unrelated to the war only if they are expressly stated.
Vattel's refusal to distinguish major from minor articles, since breach of the least article frees the other party, is Wolff § 1024's rule that peace is broken even by violating minor articles.
Both concern not refusing enemy envoys, but Wolff speaks only of manifest necessity such as peace offers, while Vattel's general maxim and its exceptions are not in this passage.

'Personne morale' with its own will, rights and duties is stock (Pufendorf); Vattel's 'capable d'obligations & de droits' matches Wolff's Praefatio ('personae morales ... subjecta jurium & obligationum').
'Personne morale' is stock; Vattel's moral person with its own understanding and will follows Wolff's Jus gentium §§ 2, 56-57.
Vattel's 'n'est originairement ... que le droit de la nature appliqué aux nations' is Wolff JG Prol. §3 ('originarie ... Jus naturae ad Gentes applicatum'); Burlamaqui gives the Hobbesian formula.

Vattel's inference (nations are free persons, so natural law must be applied to them) follows Wolff's Jus gentium §§ 2-3, which his next clause translates; Burlamaqui's phrasing is the same commonplace.
Vattel's preface names Hobbes and Pufendorf II.3.23 as targets, and Burlamaqui copies that sentence verbatim; Vattel's correction follows Wolff's Praefatio.

labelCheck.reason: Same sentence frame 'le droit des gens n'est autre chose que ... appliqué(e)', with natural law and nations substituted for sociability and non-individuals.

audit.reason: Vattel's § 7 translates Wolff's Jus gentium § 4, and the reason that states are made of men still bound by natural law echoes Wolff; 'composés d'hommes' is a commonplace.
Vattel's inference (necessary law is natural law applied, natural law is immutable, so necessary law is immutable) is Wolff JG Prol. §5; Burlamaqui only states it in passing.
Vattel's rule that treaties or customs contrary to necessary law are illegitimate follows Wolff's Prolegomena (§6); Burlamaqui's point that usages may be unjust is a different, general remark.
Both state a general duty of states to promote other states' good as far as they can, but Vattel's Wolffian 'bonheur et perfection' formula has no specific link to Burlamaqui's passage.
Priority of duties to oneself is Wolff JG §206 ('officium gentis erga seipsam vincit'); Burlamaqui's ranked rule, qualified 'toutes choses égales', is common stock.

The limit that a duty to another nation ceases when it would harm oneself follows Wolff's Jus gentium §§ 156, 206 (duty to self prevails in a collision); Burlamaqui states the stock condition on imperfect duties.
The natural liberty and independence of nations is a stock premise, here from Wolff (Jus gentium § 2; Inst. § 1089) and Vattel's own Prelim. §§ 4-5.
Vattel's definition translates Wolff's Institutiones § 80 (jus cogendi alterum si obligationi satisfacere nolit); Burlamaqui gives the stock coercion-based definition in different words.

Only the terms match: Burlamaqui's internal/external obligation is reason versus a superior's command, while Vattel's is conscience versus obligation towards others producing rights, in Wolff's sense.
Both deny that usages bind universally, but Vattel's sentence translates Wolff Prol. § 24, and Burlamaqui's point (usages not obligatory by themselves) differs in substance.
The union of distinct states under one king is Pufendorf VII.5.17 (and Grotius I.3.7), which Burlamaqui repeats; Vattel adds his own Neuchatel example.
Burlamaqui's sentence copies Pufendorf VII.5.18 ('n'exercer que d'un commun consentement certaines parties de la Souveraineté'); Vattel's paragraph opens from Grotius I.3.7.
Fundamental laws as those fixing the form of government and the manner of governing is a common definition; Vattel drops Burlamaqui's contractual frame and nothing specific ties them.
'Opposer la force à la violence' is a stock phrase of the resistance debate; Vattel's paragraph follows Grotius I.4 and Barbeyrac's notes.
The rhetorical question comes from Barbeyrac's note 4 on Grotius II.7.27 ('Or qui peut mieux juger de cela que le Peuple même?'), which Burlamaqui copies and which Vattel is answering there.
Barbeyrac's same note on Grotius II.7.27 already has the people, back in interim independence, decide by itself 'ou ceux qui le représentent'; Burlamaqui restates it.
The phrase is Pufendorf VII.7.12 ('nez d'un Mariage conforme aux Loix du Païs'), which Burlamaqui copies; Vattel's clause is as close to Pufendorf.
That conquest without the conquered's consent leaves the state of war in being is Barbeyrac's note on Grotius (and Locke), which Burlamaqui copies; nothing points to Burlamaqui.

The idea that without consent or lawful government the state of war continues after conquest is common stock; Burlamaqui's clause itself copies Barbeyrac's note on Grotius, and Vattel's condition differs.
That power is entrusted to the prince only for the public good is a commonplace; Vattel applies his own § 39 to the power of naming a successor, and the shared words are generic.

labelCheck.reason: Same phrase 'les nécessités et les commodités de la vie' with 'et même les agrémens' inserted.

audit.reason: Burlamaqui's sentence copies Pufendorf VII.9.11 ('il ne doit rien négliger, pour procurer l'entretien & l'augmentation des biens'), so the frame Vattel shares is Pufendorf's.
'Natural law applied to nations' is a stock formula that Vattel's preface traces to Hobbes and Pufendorf; nothing ties this sentence to Burlamaqui in particular.
Religion's effect on society giving the sovereign authority over it is the common jus circa sacra argument, and the wording is different.
Same argument against clerical independence in nearly the same words ('établir deux puissances indépendantes dans une même société'), not found in Pufendorf or Grotius.
Pardon as a sovereign right exercised for public utility is stock doctrine, and Burlamaqui's sentence is Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VII.4.4 word for word; nothing ties Vattel to Burlamaqui.

labelCheck.reason: Same sentence shape 'X des particuliers [font] la force de l'Etat', with biens for richesses and augmentent for sont.

audit.reason: Burlamaqui's presumed stipulation for citizens' children is Pufendorf VII.2.20 (Barbeyrac) verbatim, and Vattel's wording follows neither closely, so the shared doctrine cannot be traced to Burlamaqui.

labelCheck.reason: Same phrase 'quitter la patrie sans la permission du souverain' with 'entiérement' and 'expresse' added.

audit.reason: Vattel's passage is about taxes supplementing an insufficient domain; the source passage distinguishes goods for the king's upkeep from goods for state expenses.

Both mention public goods for the sovereign's upkeep and state expenses, but Burlamaqui distinguishes royal domain from public treasury while Vattel's point is that taxes are reserved to the nation; a commonplace overlap.

Burlamaqui's sentence is Pufendorf VIII.5.7 (Barbeyrac) verbatim, 'en même tems' included, and Vattel's claim that eminent domain is part of the empire follows Wolff (JG § 104); Burlamaqui only repeats the doctrine.
Abandoning a part of the state in extreme necessity, though it may not be alienated, comes from Barbeyrac's note 1 to Grotius II.6.6, which Burlamaqui paraphrases; the sentences differ in structure.
The abandoned part's right to defend itself 'si elle peut' is Barbeyrac's note to Grotius II.6.6, which Burlamaqui copies; Vattel words it differently, so the source cannot be told.
Same claim as Barbeyrac's note to Grotius II.6.6, and Vattel's 'le nouveau maître qu'on voudroit lui donner' is closer to Barbeyrac ('auquel on veut la donner') than to Burlamaqui.

Only the generic consent of 'the people or its representatives' is shared (Grotius III.20.5 has the rule); Vattel makes it conditional on the fundamental law and lets an absolute prince cede, unlike Burlamaqui's flat rule.

The ends of punishment (deter the offender, intimidate others) are commonplace, and Burlamaqui's sentence is Barbeyrac's Locke quotation in the note to Pufendorf VIII.3, so nothing is specific to Burlamaqui.

Vattel's non-intervention sentence translates Wolff JG § 256 ('nullus Rector civitatis habet jus regimini alieno se immiscendi'); Burlamaqui only states the common principle, in the context of punitive war.

The doctrine that foreigners may aid subjects only when tyranny justifies their own resistance is Pufendorf VIII.6.14 (Barbeyrac), which Burlamaqui copies verbatim; Vattel shares it with that common source.

labelCheck.reason: Same clause frame 'tous [ses/les] droits ... lui deviendroient inutiles' closing the same argument that rights are useless without coercion.

audit.reason: 'Opposer la force à quiconque' attacks one's rights is a stock statement of the right of defence; Burlamaqui uses it as an example of perfect rights.

Vattel's brief sentence (demand justice of the culprit's sovereign) matches only the stock punish-or-deliver rule of Grotius II.21.4, which Burlamaqui copies from Barbeyrac; no wording is paraphrased.

Punish or deliver up at the offended sovereign's request is Grotius's maxim (II.21.4), which Burlamaqui copies; nothing ties Vattel to Burlamaqui, and Vattel's wording differs too much for a close paraphrase.
Tolls that compensate road upkeep are in Pufendorf III.3.7 (Barbeyrac: 'on se dédommage ... des frais ... entretenir les chemins'), which Vattel's wording matches as well as Burlamaqui's.
Vattel recalls his own Prelim. § 6, which translates Wolff's Jus gentium § 3 ('non est nisi jus naturae ad gentes applicatum'); Burlamaqui states the same common definition.

labelCheck.reason: Same frame 'le droit des gens n'est autre chose que' plus the application of natural law to nations, reworded from Burlamaqui's sociability formula.

audit.reason: Vattel names Grotius II.15.5 here and copies Barbeyrac's wording exactly ('tenu', where Burlamaqui has 'obligé'), so the source is Grotius and Burlamaqui is a parallel copy.

The ancients' need for such treaties comes from Grotius II.15.5 (cited by Vattel) and Pufendorf VIII.9.2, which Burlamaqui paraphrases; Vattel's 'not among their allies' is closer to Grotius and Pufendorf than to Burlamaqui's 'Concitoyens'.
Vattel's point that treaties of non-injury are useful among nations who think they may harm foreigners follows Wolff JG § 392; Burlamaqui only repeats Pufendorf VIII.9.2 on the ancients.

Vattel's argument (non-injury treaties not necessary but useful, since contracted obligation binds more firmly) follows Wolff JG § 392-393; Burlamaqui's 'ne sont pas nécessaires' paraphrases Pufendorf VIII.9.2.
Vattel's definition follows Wolff JG § 395 ('eadem aut aequivalentia'), and Burlamaqui's is Pufendorf VIII.9.3 almost word for word; the proportion clause is common to that stock.

The division by the side of the inequality, with 'du côté de la Puissance la plus considérable', is Barbeyrac's Grotius II.15.7.2 verbatim, which Burlamaqui copies; Wolff JG § 398 has the same division.
Vattel's definition of unequal treaties renders Wolff JG § 398 ('eadem aut aequivalentia non promittuntur'); Burlamaqui only repeats Pufendorf VIII.9.4.
The division into personal and real treaties is stock (Grotius II.16.16, Pufendorf VIII.9.6, Wolff JG § 412).
The rule that a treaty with a republic is real is stock. Vattel's 'toute alliance ... réelle de sa nature' matches Pufendorf VIII.ix.6 more closely than Burlamaqui's 'tout traité'.
Burlamaqui copies Barbeyrac's Grotius II.16.16.2 ('changé de Républicain en Monarchique ... ne laisse pas de subsister'), which Vattel follows along with Wolff JG § 416; nothing points to Burlamaqui.
The exception for two republics allied to keep their liberty is Grotius II.16.16.2 and Pufendorf VIII.9.6; Burlamaqui only repeats it.
Burlamaqui's presumption is Barbeyrac's note 6 to Grotius II.16.16 (after Thomasius) verbatim, and Vattel, following Wolff JG § 423-424, states it only 'd'abord' and then qualifies it.
Vattel's rule matches Wolff JG § 417 ('in perpetuum, aut ad certum tempus ... reale est') and Grotius II.16.16.4 ('certain tems limité') more closely than Burlamaqui's 'certain nombre d'années'.
'Pour lui & ses Successeurs ... on voit assez par là que le Traité est réel' is Barbeyrac's Grotius II.16.16.4 verbatim, which Burlamaqui copies; Vattel follows that common source.
Burlamaqui copies Grotius II.15.14 (Barbeyrac): 'car une nouvelle obligation ne se présume pas aisément'; Vattel's phrase can come from Grotius as well, and his rule follows Wolff JG § 433.

Vattel's 'actes ... qui ne peuvent être faits qu'en vertu du traité' renders Wolff JG § 433 ('quod nonnisi vi ejusdem fieri poterat'); Burlamaqui only repeats Grotius II.15.14's exception, in a different sentence.

The annual-payment example is Barbeyrac's note 2 to Grotius II.15.14, which Burlamaqui copies verbatim; Vattel, who uses Barbeyrac's Grotius in the next §§, reworks it (continued, not renewed), so nothing points to Burlamaqui.
Vattel's choice between compelling the ally and breaking the treaty, with arms as the only means of compulsion, follows Wolff JG § 430 note; Burlamaqui only states Grotius II.15.15's stock rule.
Vattel names Grotius and quotes Barbeyrac's Grotius II.15.15 word for word ('tous les articles du traité'); Burlamaqui only repeats the same sentence ('d'un traité').

Vattel's clause matches Barbeyrac's Grotius II.15.15 exactly ('ne le rompra point', 'qu'une des parties'), where Burlamaqui differs ('pas entièrement', 'l'une des parties'): Vattel ('Il ajoute') follows Grotius, not Burlamaqui.
Stock doctrine; Vattel's distinction of conventions by subordinate powers under express order or within their office follows Wolff JG § 464, and the wording differs from Burlamaqui's.
Reserved ratification must be express is Grotius II.15.17.2 with Barbeyrac's note 1 ('on entend par là ... une ratification expresse'), closer to Vattel's 'comme cela s'entend' than Burlamaqui is.
Stock rule (Grotius II.15.16.3; Wolff JG §§ 465, 468: sponsio binds only if ratified expressly or tacitly), which Vattel follows; Burlamaqui only states it.
Tacit ratification by acts referable to no other cause is Grotius II.15.17.3 and Wolff JG § 468, which Vattel follows; Burlamaqui repeats the commonplace.

Vattel's definition of sponsio translates Wolff JG § 465 ('sine mandato potestatis summae, nec intra fines praepositionis' = 'hors des termes de sa commission, et sans ordre'); Burlamaqui gives the stock Grotian definition in other words.
Vattel follows Wolff JG § 470 (silence alone is no ratification; dissent should be declared as soon as the sovereign learns of the sponsio); Burlamaqui only states the same Grotian point.

labelCheck.reason: Same phrase 'jusqu'à l'accomplissement de ce' about hostages, with only the relative clause reworded.

audit.reason: Vattel's passage (only liberty pledged; hostages kept captive, not killed; killing them an error about a right over life) follows Wolff JG §§ 501, 532; Burlamaqui states the common doctrine.
Hostages free once the engagement is fulfilled is Wolff JG § 502, which Vattel follows; a commonplace in Burlamaqui.
That the sovereign may compel subjects to be hostages is a stock Grotian point, and the wording differs too much for a close paraphrase.
Vattel's ground (burdens borne equally by citizens) follows Wolff JG § 536 (obses solus id gratis subire non tenetur); Burlamaqui states indemnity in other words.
Burlamaqui copies Pufendorf VIII.8.6 (Barbeyrac); Vattel's rule with an equivalent substitute and his argument that the treaty did not make the king a hostage follow Wolff JG § 519.
Burlamaqui's reason is Barbeyrac's note 2 to Pufendorf VIII.8.6; Vattel's presumption of the state's non-consent matches Wolff JG § 519 and that note as much as Burlamaqui.
Both hold that the sovereign who breaks faith cannot make hostages answer for it with their lives, and the next row shows both go on to make the hostage a mere prisoner.
Hostage kept as captive (perpetual captivity) after breach of faith follows Wolff JG § 532; Burlamaqui only states the common rule.
Vattel's illicit-case exception is Grotius II.16.26.3 and the tacit just-war clause of alliances Wolff JG §§ 659-660; no aid in a manifestly unjust war is stock doctrine (also Pufendorf VIII.6.14).

Vattel's exceptions follow Grotius II.16.27 (aid not owed when one needs one's forces for one's own defence); Burlamaqui's not perishing with an ally echoes Pufendorf VIII.6.14, a related but general point.
Both texts give the same first condition of reprisals (the wrong or debt must be evident), followed by the prior demand for justice, but in different words.
Clear cause and justice first sought is Grotius III.2.5, Wolff JG § 589 and Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VIII.6.13, which Burlamaqui follows; 'en venir' is a common idiom, not shared wording.

Vattel's first ground (only state to state are citizens' goods the nation's) is Wolff JG §§ 589-590; the reprisals-as-prelude-to-war argument is Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VIII.6.13, which Burlamaqui repeats.

Vattel's definition of public war translates Wolff JG § 607 ('quod geritur inter gentes, seu auctoribus iis, qui summum imperium habent'); Burlamaqui's sentence is a remark on restricting the word 'guerre'.

Restricting a law-of-nations treatise to public war is a generic scoping remark; 'dont nous avons à traiter ici' is a stock formula and the source passage lacks Vattel's assignment of private war to natural law.
Burlamaqui copies Pufendorf VIII.6.3's division of offensive war; Vattel's three ends (claim, punishment, prevention) follow Wolff JG §§ 615-619.

Vattel translates Wolff JG § 745 ('Bellum publicum sine militibus geri non posse... jus conscribendi militem') and § 747 (droit de majesté); Burlamaqui only states the same inference in a different sentence.

Same doctrine, but Vattel's sequence (all bound, unfit excepted, those with useful and necessary functions exempt unless necessity presses, clergy) follows Wolff JG §§ 749-752; Burlamaqui's 'aucun citoyen ne peut s'exempter de prendre les armes' is only a parallel statement.
Vattel's definition follows Wolff JG § 621 (justificae from right 'quibus evincitur', suasoriae 'ab utilitate'); Burlamaqui only relays Grotius's raisons justificatives / motifs distinction.

Vattel's sentence translates Wolff JG § 619 ('Fines duo priores intenduntur in bello offensivo; tertius in defensivo'); Burlamaqui gives Pufendorf's definition of offensive war (VIII.6.3) almost verbatim.
Vattel's concurrence of honest motives with justificative reasons and the justice/prudence pairing follow Wolff JG §§ 621-623; the Burlamaqui passage only states Grotius's distinction.

Vattel naming apparent justificative reasons 'prétextes' follows Wolff JG §§ 624-625 (rationes quasi justificae 'tantummodo praetextus sunt'); Burlamaqui's third kind of unjust war is the common Grotius/Pufendorf classification.

Vattel follows Wolff JG § 629 ('injustum vero est defensivum si offensivum fuerit justum') and § 972; Burlamaqui copies Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VIII.6.3 almost word for word, and its sentence form differs from Vattel's.

Vattel's argument (nations independent, no judge, so both sides' arms count as legitimate as to effects) is Wolff JG § 888; Burlamaqui shares only Grotius's phrase 'effets extérieurs' (III.6.2), and he applies it to acquiring property, not to doubtful causes.
Vattel's syllogism (war allowed only for injury, so growth of power alone gives no right) is Wolff JG § 640; Burlamaqui, after Grotius II.1.17, only states the same rule.
The power-plus-will condition comes from Grotius II.22.5 and is common stock; nothing in Vattel's wording points to Burlamaqui's Droit politique rather than Grotius.

Vattel's declaration as a last attempt to end the dispute without bloodshed is Wolff JG § 710, and 'exposer le sujet' matches Wolff § 740 ('rationes justificae exponuntur'); Burlamaqui's statement of the purpose is generic.

Vattel follows Wolff JG §§ 708-709 (conditional declaration joined to repetitio rerum, no new pure declaration needed); Burlamaqui copies Grotius III.3.7, and its sentence is not shaped like Vattel's.

Vattel's frame follows Wolff's Jus gentium § 707 and points back to his own Prelim. § 26; the 'binding until renounced' clause is also in Barbeyrac's note on Pufendorf II.3.23, and nothing here is specific to Burlamaqui.

Publication of war to one's own subjects is in Wolff JG § 737 (publicatio, distinct from denunciatio); Burlamaqui only shares the general point, without Vattel's specifics (dating of rights, effects in the peace treaty).

Different point: Vattel's 'the nation can only blame itself' if it refuses envoys is Wolff JG § 714 ('qui culpa sua eam reddidit impossibilem'); Burlamaqui says modes of declaration are arbitrary provided the prince cannot be ignorant of it.

Vattel's passage on declaring at the frontier and on the aim of the declaration follows Wolff JG § 716 ('non alio fine denunciandum, quam ut pars adversa... bellum avertere possit'); Burlamaqui's statement of the aim is generic.

Vattel's § 64 (publication to other powers, 'tel ou tel peuple' = 'cum hac vel ista Gente', manifestos with justificative reasons, orders to subjects) follows Wolff JG §§ 737-740; Burlamaqui's publication to subjects shares only the general idea.
Vattel names Grotius and quotes Grotius-Barbeyrac I.3.4 verbatim, including 'selon le droit des gens' and 'de part et d'autre', which Burlamaqui's copy of the same formula leaves out.
Vattel follows Wolff JG § 728: the thing's nature depends on the owner and not on the place, enemy ships, and the presumption until proof; Burlamaqui gives Grotius III.6.5-6 doctrine only.

Vattel's rule (aid to a just war allowed and even owed, none to an unjust one) translates Wolff JG § 656; Burlamaqui, copying Grotius II.25.4, only says one cannot innocently aid a manifestly unjust war.
Vattel's ban on alliances with a party to an unjust war, then weighing the good of the state, follows Wolff JG §§ 658-659; Burlamaqui only gives the Grotian commonplace.

No duty to aid an ally in a manifestly unjust war is common stock (Grotius II.15.13 and II.25.4, Pufendorf VIII.6.14), and Vattel cross-refers to his own §§ 86-89; the two sentences are shaped differently.

Burlamaqui here copies Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VIII.6.7; Vattel's two-part impartiality rule also follows Wolff JG § 678 (no troops, arms, supplies) and § 683 ('quod uni praestatur, id praestandum quoque alteri').

Vattel's § 118 (offices owed outside war, access and purchase for both sides' subjects, exception by treaty) follows Wolff JG §§ 683-684; Burlamaqui's 'service d'humanité' rule is Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VIII.6.7 copied.

Opposite rules: Burlamaqui (Barbeyrac's note) forbids supplying war goods to either side unless an engagement permits it, while Vattel lets both sides buy everything unless a neutrality treaty forbids war goods, which is Wolff JG § 683 ('nisi expresse aliter conventum').

Same specific rule: in extreme necessity seize a neutral place and restore it as soon as the danger passes, paying the damage (Grotius II.2.10 has no payment); the wording is identical in Barbeyrac's note to Pufendorf VIII.6.7, which Burlamaqui copies, so either may be the source.

The equal-treatment rule is common (Wolff JG §§ 683-684, Barbeyrac's note which Burlamaqui copies); Vattel's exception for changed circumstances differs from Burlamaqui's 'raison manifeste' for favours not owed.

Same stock rule that no hostility may be done on neutral soil, which Grotius III.4.8 states; Vattel grounds it in his own territorial-sovereignty principle, and only the phrase 'aucun acte d'hostilité' is shared.
Burlamaqui restates Grotius's first rule (III.1.2); Vattel's end-justifies-necessary-means wording follows Wolff, Jus gentium § 613.
Sparing old men, women and children is the common Grotian temperamentum; the wording and grounds differ, since Vattel rests it on their offering no resistance.
The Leonidas sentence is Barbeyrac's Grotius III.4.18 word for word, which Burlamaqui copies; Vattel's Justin reference is Grotius's marginal note, and he follows Grotius through the whole section.
Vattel follows Grotius III.4.15, which he cites in the same sentence ('Il est de l'intérêt commun des Nations, qu'on ne donne point de tels exemples'); Burlamaqui only copies it.
The Scaevola praise and Vattel's references (Livy, Cicero, Valerius Maximus) come from Grotius III.4.18; Burlamaqui only abridges the same sentence.
Vattel's weaken-the-enemy, strengthen-ourselves argument follows Wolff § 823; Burlamaqui copies Pufendorf VIII.6.17 on keeping captured goods up to the debt and war costs, which is stock doctrine.
Burlamaqui copies Pufendorf VIII.6.18 (booty belongs first to the sovereign); Vattel's reasons (soldiers and auxiliaries are his instruments) follow Wolff §§ 852-854, and the wording is not close.
Sparing temples, public buildings and tombs that do not weaken the enemy is Grotius III.12.5-7, which Vattel cites in the same paragraph (Belisarius); Burlamaqui only condenses it.
Vattel's rule that needless hostility is 'licence' echoes Wolff § 926; Burlamaqui only restates Grotius's general rule from the other side.
Vattel's 'tout lien d'humanité est rompu' is Barbeyrac's phrase (note 11 on Grotius III.4.18), and 'men remain men' is Grotius III.19.1; Burlamaqui states the same doctrine in other words.

Vattel's 'mettre des bornes à ses fureurs ... ses maux n'auroient plus de bornes' follows Barbeyrac's note 3 on Pufendorf VIII.7.2, and the capitulating towns follow Grotius III.19.1; Burlamaqui only states the common-interest doctrine.
